questions.q: How does the LPT (Longest Processing Time first) heuristic work?
options: Always assign the largest item to group A and the smallest to group B
Randomly assign each item to a group and repeat until balanced
Sort all items in decreasing order, then assign each one, in that order, to whichever group currently has the smaller total
Run a quantum circuit to decide each assignment
questions.explain: LPT is a simple, deterministic classical heuristic: sort items descending by size, then greedily place each one into whichever group currently has less total, in that sorted order.

questions.q: What result did LPT achieve on the capstone's Number Partitioning problem (d=[3,5,2,4]), and how did it compare to the true optimum?
options: LPT required hundreds of iterations to converge to the optimum
LPT found an 8-6 split, missing the true optimum by 2
LPT failed to produce any valid assignment
LPT found a 7-7 split (imbalance=0), matching the true optimum exactly, in a single deterministic pass
questions.explain: Sorting d=[3,5,2,4] descending (5,4,3,2) and greedily assigning to the smaller-total group gave A=7, B=7 -- a perfect, zero-imbalance split matching the true optimum, found in one deterministic pass with no search needed.

questions.q: According to the lesson's fairness-checklist application, why does judging LPT and QAOA by 'expected cost across repeated runs' require extra care?
options: Because QAOA is also fully deterministic, making the comparison trivial
Because expected cost is undefined for any classical algorithm

Because LPT is deterministic -- it gives the same answer every time on this instance -- so 'expected cost across repeated runs' isn't a meaningful metric for it the way it is for QAOA's probabilistic output
Because LPT cannot be run more than once under any circumstances
questions.explain: LPT produces the identical result every run since it has no randomness, while QAOA's output is a probability distribution -- so applying the same 'expected cost over repeated runs' metric to both sides needs this distinction made explicit, exactly the kind of care Lesson 21's fairness checklist demands.

questions.q: Why does the lesson insist that 'classical won this round' is the right finding to report, rather than something to downplay?
options: Because classical methods always outperform quantum methods on every possible problem, so this result is unsurprising and uninteresting
Because the QAOA result from Lesson 25 was computed incorrectly and should be discarded

Because reporting an honest result -- even one unfavorable to the quantum method -- is exactly the discipline Chapter 5 built an entire benchmarking methodology around, and it matches the broader pattern that quantum methods haven't demonstrated an advantage at this scale
Because reporting negative results is required by law in academic publishing
questions.explain: The lesson frames this honest, specific, from-scratch result as consistent with (not an exception to) the course's consistent finding: current quantum optimization methods haven't shown an advantage over strong classical baselines at this scale -- and reporting it plainly is the actual professional skill being modeled.

questions.q: What does testing LPT on d=[5,6,4,1,9,8] (where the true optimal imbalance is 1, via the split {9,8} vs {6,5,4,1}) demonstrate about LPT as a general-purpose heuristic?
options: This counterexample proves LPT is mathematically equivalent to brute force
LPT always finds the true optimum on every possible instance, with no exceptions

LPT is not mathematically guaranteed to find the true optimum on every instance -- it can produce a worse imbalance than the true optimum on some inputs, even though it succeeded on the lesson's original 4-task example
LPT cannot be applied to instances with more than 4 numbers
questions.explain: This instance is a verified counterexample where LPT's greedy sort-and-assign procedure does not reach the true optimal imbalance of 1 -- showing that LPT's success on the capstone's specific 4-task instance doesn't generalize to a guarantee of optimality on every instance.
